footer.aboutText: SemantIC checks AI-generated images before publication for physical coherence, semantic consistency and bias – and shows you verifiable cues where an image may not hold, in substance, what its impression promises. Read more under {link}.
footer.projectText: SemantIC is the teaching project of the bachelor's thesis “Visual Bias in the AI-generated Image” (Multimedia Production, FH Graubünden). It is a review assistant for content professionals, not a fake detector – a research prototype that is being developed empirically.

thirdParties.usaBody: With Google, Anthropic, Modal and Vercel, a data transfer to the USA takes place. Google, Anthropic and Vercel are certified under the Swiss-U.S. Data Privacy Framework (DPF). Switzerland has recognized the DPF as an adequacy mechanism – transfer to DPF-certified US companies is therefore permitted under the revDSG. Modal is not DPF-certified; here the transfer relies on the EU Standard Contractual Clauses (SCC) in Modal's data processing agreement, which explicitly includes Swiss data protection law. The rate-limit counter at Upstash is located in the EU region; no transfer to a third country takes place here.

cookies.title: Cookies and tracking
cookies.p1: SemantIC uses {no} tracking – no Google Analytics, no Plausible, no Matomo, no advertising cookies, no third-party cookies.
cookies.p2: SemantIC sets exactly two cookies, both purely functional: The {bypass} – it is only set if you redeem an access code yourself, is HMAC-signed (i.e. not forgeable), contains no personal content and expires after 30 days. And the {lang} – it remembers your language choice when you switch manually, and expires after one year. Both are technically necessary for their function and serve no tracking – which is why SemantIC needs no cookie banner.

security.item2: The bypass cookie is HMAC-signed and therefore not forgeable.
security.item3: An IP-based daily limit protects against misuse.

hero.imageAlt: AI-generated café scene with a chrome espresso machine – looks like a real photo.
hero.title: The flawless image and its blind spots.
hero.lead: AI images reliably look good – and that is exactly what can hide their flaws. The scene here, too, is entirely AI-generated.

intro.lead: This page walks through four types of flaw: body and anatomy, the logic of a scene, light and space – and role imagery that cannot be pinned to any single spot in the picture. That such breaks can slip past under a convincing surface is what SemantIC calls the {effect} – {link}.
intro.linkText: it is derived under How it works
intro.body: The examples on this page come from the empirical part of the bachelor's thesis – 144 AI-generated images, systematically coded. Two of three photorealistic images among them (71 of 106) carried at least one flaw – the rule in this corpus, not an outlier. All markings below come from this manual coding, not from a fresh model run. It is a corpus of its own, not a representative cross-section of all AI images.

anatomy.title: When bodies don't fit together.
anatomy.prose: The classic among AI flaws – the rarest of the three flaw types in the corpus, but still present in dense scenes with several people. Where people overlap, the AI loses the boundary between two bodies – arms and legs merge into one another. Hands remain a problem of their own: sometimes one finger too many, sometimes one hand too many for the pose.

context.title: When the scene makes no sense.
context.prose: No magnifier and no detector finds these breaks – only a comparison with world knowledge does. A laptop with no screen, a houseplant in the coffee cup, a full wine glass at a child's place: technically rendered flawlessly, yet absurd in substance. Because the image looks clean, what is wrong only registers on a second look.

physics.title: When light and space don't add up.
physics.prose: The most common flaw type in the corpus – and usually the most subtle. Reflections that don't match the scene in front of them, screens facing the wrong way: details that barely register because the image otherwise looks convincing. This is exactly where the masking effect comes in.

stereotype.title: The flaw with no spot in the picture.
stereotype.prose: Some flaws are not a markable spot but a pattern. For “a nurse” the AI typically delivers a young, attractive woman; for “a CEO” a man in a leadership pose. Perceived gender or skin tone are in themselves {no} finding – only the stereotyped casting of the role sets it off.

closing.title: The conspicuous flaw is the exception – the subtle one is the rule.
closing.prose: Hunting for the sixth finger alone doesn't get you far: even in this corpus it is not the anatomy artefacts that dominate but physics and context breaks – and the more strongly an image is curated, the harder the flaw is to spot. Pure artefact hunting is therefore unreliable. That is why SemantIC checks not “real or fake” but the {coherence} of an image.
closing.crossref: How SemantIC forms a verdict from this is explained under {link}.

hero.title: What happens when SemantIC checks your image.
hero.lead: SemantIC takes an AI-generated image and looks at it along three dimensions: whether it is physically plausible, whether it makes sense in substance, and which clichés it carries. On this page we show you what the tool does, where its criteria come from and – just as importantly – what it deliberately does not do.

s1.title: Why good images hide their own flaws.
s1.lead: AI image generators optimize for what reads as “good” at first glance: sharpness, colour, light, composition. They optimize far less for coherence in substance – the logic of the scene, proportions, clichés. Images thus become reliably beautiful, but not reliably correct.
s1.body: The consequence is the real problem: a convincing image does not invite a closer look. The surface puts the eye at ease, and weaknesses slip through. We call this connection {masking} – the working hypothesis behind SemantIC: a convincing surface can make critical scrutiny harder. The study behind it supports this assumption; it cannot prove it.
s1.theoryBody: This effect is not just an observation; it can be placed scientifically. Recent research on AI detection systems shows that artificial neural networks prioritize visual properties, whereas humans grasp images more through their meaning. That the same holds for image generators is the assumption of this thesis. SemantIC steps into exactly this gap: it looks where the eye is satisfied too quickly.

s2.title: From image to finding.
s2.lead: SemantIC separates content and aesthetics into two distinct assessment tracks – so that appeal does not gloss over the judgment on substance. Aesthetics are estimated twice: by a vision model and an independent reference model; if the two diverge strongly, the finding says so. Only afterwards are both results brought together.
s2.note: Model-agnostic – Gemini & Claude are the current standard models, interchangeable. The aesthetic score is the average of Claude and an independent reference model (LAION Aesthetic Predictor); if the two diverge by 20 points or more, the finding says so; if the reference fails, Claude counts alone. If you provide a prompt or context, an image-text comparison (CLIP) also runs – a pure diagnostic signal with no influence on scores and traffic lights. The symbols are stylized placeholders.

s2b.title: The guardrails of the assessment.
s2b.body1: An image model on its own tends to be led by visual perfection. SemantIC therefore applies guardrails to the assessment that push towards substantiated, traceable judgments.
s2b.body2: That makes the assessment more disciplined and more traceable. Where the tool reaches its limits, SemantIC discloses that (section “We know the limits”).
s2b.note: “Masked → clear”: tendency dampened, guardrail sharp. Largely hard-enforced (fixed schema & check rules); the criteria come from 144 coded images.

s3.title: What lies behind physics, semantics and bias.

physics.body: Does the image obey the laws of nature? Light, shadow, anatomy, proportions, materials. Such breaks are often small – but they reliably give an image away once you see them.

semantics.body: Does the scene make sense – and does it fit your context? A technically clean image can still be off in substance: a situation that would not happen that way, or that does not fit your piece.

bias.body: Which roles, poses, clichés does the image show? A beautiful image of a cliché remains a cliché. Important: gender or skin tone are in themselves no finding – only a stereotyped casting of the role, power dynamic or a context break sets it off.

s4.title: When the surface is stronger than the content.
s4.body: SemantIC assesses separately how good an image looks (its aesthetics) and how well it holds up in substance (its integrity). If appeal clearly exceeds substance, that is the breeding ground for masking – the perfect surface can cover flaws before you notice them. There is deliberately no single masking metric; the quadrant shows the principle, not the result of a check.

s5.title: Why you should frame the image.
s5.body: Before SemantIC checks, we ask two things: your {stance} on the image and its {form}. Both only frame the recommendation – they shift neither the score nor the findings.
s5.haltungH3: What function does the image have?
s5.haltungHint: The same weakness weighs differently depending on whether an image shows a cliché deliberately or reproduces it unreflectively.
s5.verwendungHint: From this, SemantIC derives how strict the standard should be.
s5.note: Selection in the tool – shown here for overview only, not clickable.

s6.title: Why SemantIC proves you nothing.
s6.body: SemantIC gives no hard verdicts but reasoned cues: each finding shows where you should look more closely – not that an image is “wrong”. Whether it fits your context is not something any tool decides for you; the final judgment stays with you.
isItems: A quality and integrity assessor for AI images
A tool that shows you where to look more closely
An appraisal before publication – the decision stays with you
isNotItems: Not a fake or deepfake detector
No “real or fake” verdict about provenance
No substitute for your own editorial judgment

s7.title: We know the limits – and disclose them.
s7.body1: Every limit here has been empirically tested – in documented test series against the human coding, and for anatomy additionally blinded with a second vision model. You should know when you can rely on a finding and when your own eye is needed.

0.body: In the documented anatomy test run (16 images, 42 runs), no clean image triggered a red finding. If SemantIC shows red, take it seriously – yellow cues, by contrast, can sometimes be off.

1.body: Green means “nothing found” – not “flawless”. It focuses your visual check; it doesn't replace it.

2.h3: Anatomy: a flag is a check request
2.body: The tool finds local hand and finger artefacts more readily than structural body flaws (head, limbs, leg placement) – but it depends on the image: in the tests there were both missed and falsely reported findings, checked across two vision models. An anatomy flag is therefore a check request to you, not a diagnosis.

3.body: Severe, moderate, minor are an estimate by the vision model, not a measurement. Whether a marked point is publication-critical is decided by your own look at the image.

s7.body2: The same tests also surfaced findings that a human eye had missed. The cues complement your visual check – every finding is built to be verifiable with a marking on the image.

s8.title: Research, not generic model knowledge.
s8.body1: The check logic rests on an empirical basis of its own: a qualitative content analysis of 144 AI-generated images. From it came the recurring error profiles, the reading modes and the visual drivers the tool works with – the practical part of the bachelor's thesis “Visual Bias in the AI-generated Image” (Multimedia Production, FH Graubünden).
s8.body2: The pipeline was developed over documented iterations and tested against the human coding – the validated limits above come from exactly these tests. It is deliberately model-agnostic: criteria, evidence requirements and check rules hang on the research basis, not on an AI model. The models used are interchangeable – the check grid stays.

s9.title: What happens to your image.
s9.body: Your image is transmitted to external services for analysis and is not stored at SemantIC itself – exactly what goes to whom and how long anything is kept is set out in the privacy policy.

closing.title: Enough theory. Have an image checked

phys.body: Visible here: the stethoscope is impossibly tangled – tubing, headset and band run together in a way that could not really be worn. A structural flaw that disappears in the overall impression.

sem.body: Does the scene add up? Not here: the name badge shows a photo of a different person, name and lettering are gibberish – a context break in the middle of the image.

bias.body: Gender and skin tone are only described, never judged. What is judged is the pattern: the nurse is cast, as if it went without saying, as a young, flawless woman – a role and body cliché that image generators reproduce again and again.

blindspot.title: An image can look perfect and still not be right.
blindspot.lead: AI image generators are good at making images beautiful – and considerably worse at making them {correct}: physically plausible, fitting in substance, free of clichés. Visual perfection can cover these weaknesses: where an image convinces, the scrutinizing look is more easily left out. We call this effect {masking} – and SemantIC works against it.

head.title: Looks good. But it's wrong.
head.subtitle: What the study on AI-generated images found
head.meta: Results for the participants of the online study (April to June 2026)

s1.title: What it was about
s1.p1: AI image generators now produce images that look like photos at first glance. Yet they often contain errors: a watch with an impossible face, a misspelled sign, an object that makes no physical sense. And they frequently show stereotypical depictions, for instance when «a leader» appears as a man in a suit.
s1.p2: The question of the thesis was: {question} In the thesis, this assumption is called the «masking effect»: the beautiful surface could conceal the flawed content.
s1.p1b: The impetus for this thesis came from a study by Mahner et al. (2025): deep neural networks and humans apparently process images with different priorities. Such networks weight visual properties such as shape and colour above all, whereas humans weight the meaning of the content. This has been shown for AI systems for image recognition. My assumption was that this visual preference also carries over to image generation: that image generators produce images that are aesthetically convincing but may be distorted in content or in social terms.
s1.p2Question: Does the visual preference in AI images lead us to overlook such errors and stereotypes, or simply accept them?
s1.p3: This spring you took part in the online study on this question. You rated six images and then chose a cover image from four options for each of seven fictional articles. In total, 55 participations were included in the analysis.

s2.title: The key findings in four points

pt1.h3: All images were AI-generated. About one in two was recognised.
pt1.p1: Every one of the six images you rated came from an AI image generator. For the question «Is this image AI-generated?», the hit rate was 48 percent on average. In other words: about half of the images were not recognised as AI. Ticking «unsure» did not count as a hit.
pt1.p2: Those who did not recognise an image as AI also found it considerably more credible. Whether one causes the other cannot be determined from the data.

pt2.h3: Less credible, but on average not rejected.
pt2.p1: Four of the six images contained a content error, two were error-free. Error-free here means: free of the content errors under study, in physics, anatomy or context. Such an image can still show a stereotypical depiction.
pt2.p2: On a scale from 1 (not credible at all) to 7 (very credible), the images with errors scored lower than the error-free ones. On average they received 4.3 instead of 5.2 points. Taken together, however, they still lay above the middle of the scale. So an error cost points. But on average the images were not dismissed as not credible.
pt2.p3: This comparison applies only to these six images. With other images it could turn out differently.

pt3.h3: Not every error stands out equally.
pt3.p1: For two images you could optionally explain your rating in your own words. A large difference emerged there:
items: In the café image, the window lettering read «TEE & COFPAE» instead of «TEA & COFFEE». Of the 33 people who wrote a reason, 25 named this error.
In the portrait of a leader, the wristwatch had a physically impossible face. Of the 22 people who wrote a reason, only 4 named the error.
pt3.p2: For these two images, the lettering error was thus named far more often than the watch error. Whether this is due to the type of error cannot be said with certainty from two images. In any case, the portrait received the best credibility ratings of all four images with errors. One person wrote that they had checked the ring, fingers and suit and found no obvious errors. This is what the masking effect could look like: the image seems coherent, and the error goes unnoticed.
pt3.p3: The figures apply only to the people who wrote something. Those who wrote nothing may or may not have seen the error.

pt4.h3: In the image choice, stereotypes were rarely mentioned.
pt4.p1: In each of the seven choice sets, exactly one of the four images was free of such content errors. The other three showed a stereotypical depiction, contained a different error, or were deliberately designed against a stereotype. Under random choice, the error-free image would have won in a quarter of cases. In fact it was chosen in 39 percent of cases, i.e. more often than chance. But most choices fell on the other images, most of them distorted. It has to be said: 18 of the 28 images on offer were distorted, and one had to be chosen.
pt4.p2: More interesting than the choice itself were the reasons, which were required for every choice. Most often, participants justified their choice by saying that an image looked «real» or «natural», that it matched the article title, or that it looked good. Of the 212 reasons given for a distorted image, only 8 mentioned a stereotype or a social norm at all. That does not mean nobody saw the stereotypes. But they were almost never mentioned.

figureCeo.caption: The portrait looked convincing to most. The error sits in the detail: the watch face is physically impossible.

s3.title: A look behind the scenes: the image analysis
s3.p1: Before the online study, I examined 144 AI images one by one. They come from 12 image prompts given to three image generators (as of February 2026), four images per prompt and generator. For each image I recorded how realistic it looks and whether it contains errors or stereotypes.
s3.p2: More than half were «beautiful and wrong»: 77 of the 144 images looked realistic and still contained at least one error or stereotype. Exactly this combination is the precondition for a masking effect to occur at all. Realistic here does not mean glossy. The images were convincing in different ways, as a magazine photo, as a snapshot, as a film scene or as a reportage image. Precisely images that look like imperfect snapshots often appeared realistic in the analysis.
s3.p3: Stereotypes appeared above all where the prompt was vague. 40 of the 144 images showed a stereotypical depiction, 23 of them for brief prompts such as «a CEO». Where the prompt explicitly asked for a non-stereotypical depiction, the generators delivered it in 18 of 24 cases. The prompt itself was almost always fulfilled: 98 percent of the images implemented it completely. Errors and stereotypes still occurred.

s4.title: What does this mean?
s4.p1: The results point to a limited masking effect that depends on the individual image. Images with errors were rated lower, but on average not rejected. The watch error was rarely named, the lettering error often. And in the image choice, participants justified their decision above all by how real and fitting an image looked. Whether it plays into stereotypical role images hardly came up.
s4.p1b: The findings do not contradict this assumption: the images were visually convincing across all styles. But they do not prove the mechanism behind it.
s4.p2: For everyone who works with images, this means: that an AI image looks good says nothing about whether it is correct. Anyone using such images must check them for content: text in the image, hands, objects, reflections, and just as much the question of whom the image shows and how.
s4.p3: And in everyday life? First impressions are not to be trusted. Even those who look closely can miss an error, as the example of the watch shows.

s5.title: How the study was run and where its limits lie
items: 79 people started the study; 55 complete participations by people aged 18 to 65 were analysed.
Participants were recruited through personal networks and online communities. The results apply to this group, not to «the population».

All images shown were of high visual quality. So the study shows how high-quality AI images are rated, not what quality does compared with poor images. That the beautiful surface conceals the errors is therefore an interpretation, not proof.
In the cover image choice, an image had to be chosen even if none appealed. Some wrote as much in their reasons.
The images come from three generators as of February 2026. Newer models may behave differently.

s6.title: The answer: which images were error-free?
s6.intro: Error-free here means: free of the content errors under study. An error-free image can still show a stereotypical depiction.
